claims.text: Template-assisted dealloying followed by controlled solvothermal treatment can form three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
Machine-learning optimization of synthesis parameters will enable precise atomic ordering in the resulting nanoframeworks.
The proposed synthesis will maximize the number of catalytically active sites.
The starting bulk or precursor NM-HEA has a multielement composition.
The starting bulk or precursor NM-HEA has non-uniform atomic ordering.
Reaction kinetics, pH, temperature, and selective-etching conditions can be optimized by a machine-learning model for this synthesis.
Machine-learning-guided tuning of solvothermal parameters can steer selective etching and atomic reorganization.
Selective dissolution of particular elements and controlled atomic rearrangement produce the three-dimensional nanoframe structure.
A machine-learning model can map synthesis parameters to dealloying kinetics with sufficient accuracy for precise process control.
Solvothermal selective etching preferentially removes less-noble components from the NM-HEA.
Selective etching promotes atomic-level reorganization of the remaining metals.
Atomic reorganization and selective etching assemble a porous, high-surface-area nanoframework.
A porous nanoframework with more exposed structural sites is advantageous for catalysis.
The proposed process will yield a uniform three-dimensional NM-HEA architecture with enhanced atomic mixing.
The proposed material will have a higher density of catalytically active sites than conventionally synthesized structures.
Conventional NM-HEA synthesis produces bulk alloys with uncontrolled phase separation.
Conventional NM-HEA structures expose active sites less efficiently than the proposed nanoframework.
Success depends on tight control of dealloying and solvothermal conditions and on adequate machine-learning predictive accuracy.
Failure to improve atomic ordering, active-site exposure, or catalytic performance relative to a non-optimized control would falsify the hypothesis.
